problemText: A satellite image is a picture of the ground taken from which location?
choices: From a camera on a satellite far out in space above Earth
From a camera in an aircraft flying close to the ground
From a drawing made by a mapmaker sitting at a desk
From a camera on the ground pointing upward at the sky
hints: The name 'satellite image' gives you a clue about where the camera is located.
This picture is taken from much higher up than an aerial photograph.

problemText: A mapmaker draws a map of a city park. The mapmaker labels the park's name, the walking paths, and the benches. At the exact same time, a photographer in an airplane takes an aerial view of the same park and captures the grass, trees, paths, benches, and a person sleeping on one of the benches. Which feature appears in the aerial view but is least likely to appear on the mapmaker's map?
choices: The walking paths, because they are drawn features that mapmakers always include
The person sleeping on the bench, because the mapmaker did not plan for anyone to be there at that moment
The park's name, because it is a label made of letters and words rather than a physical object on the ground
The trees, because they change size and shape throughout the year depending on the season
hints: Remember that a picture records whatever is physically present at that exact moment, whether or not it was planned for.
A map shows only what a mapmaker chose to draw ahead of time.

problemText: A student looks at a satellite image of a coast and sees where the land ends and the ocean begins. She then looks at a map of the same coast. On the map, she sees a line marking where one country's territory ends and another country's territory begins, drawn right along the coast. Why does the satellite image show the land-and-ocean edge but the map must draw the country boundary line?
choices: Because satellite images can only record natural features that reflect light, while maps are tools designed by people to represent human decisions like where boundaries should be drawn
Because the satellite image was taken from a camera that is programmed to ignore boundary lines, whereas mapmakers are trained to draw every single line they see on the ground
Because the land and ocean are real physical features that appear in pictures, while a country boundary is a line a person drew on a map to show a choice
Because satellites are positioned too high in space to detect thin painted lines on the ground, so mapmakers must add boundary lines that cannot be seen from orbit
hints: Think about what is actually painted or marked on the ground itself.
One of these lines is a real physical feature; the other exists only because someone decided to draw it.

problemText: A city builds a new road last month. Today, a satellite image of the city is taken, and a cartographer finishes drawing an updated map of the city. The satellite image clearly shows the new road as a paved surface, but the cartographer's new map does not include the road. Which two reasons together best explain why the new road appears in one but not the other?
choices: The road is made of dark asphalt that satellites can easily photograph, but the cartographer used an old map that was drawn before the road was built
Satellite images can only show new roads, while maps can only show old roads, so the two tools show completely different things
The satellite camera captured the road because it took the picture on a sunny day, but the cartographer's map was incomplete because it rained while she was drawing it
The satellite image records whatever physical feature exists at that moment, but the map only shows features the mapmaker chose to draw, and the mapmaker may not have known about the new road yet
hints: A picture captures whatever is actually there on the ground right now; a map reflects what a person decided to include.
The mapmaker may have completed the map before finding out about the new road, or may have chosen not to include it.

problemText: A student claims that an aerial view is exactly the same thing as a satellite image, just with a different name, and that therefore a satellite image can show everything a map can show. Which part of this claim is wrong, and why?
choices: Both parts are wrong; the two pictures are taken from different heights, and neither picture can show a boundary line that has no physical mark on the ground
Only the second part is wrong; satellite images and aerial views are truly the same tool, but no picture can show a boundary line with no physical mark on the ground
Only the first part is wrong; aerial views and satellite images are taken from different heights, but both pictures can show invisible boundary lines that maps can draw
Neither part is wrong; they describe the same tool, and that tool can indeed show everything a map shows, only better
hints: Check what makes a satellite image different from an aerial view in terms of where the camera is located.
Then check whether any picture, no matter how clear, can capture a line that is not physically painted or marked on the ground.

problemText: A nature preserve has a stream running through it. The stream flows out of the preserve and into a river that forms the boundary between two states. A satellite image taken today shows the stream clearly and the river's path, but shows no line separating one state from the other. A map of the preserve shows the stream, the river, the state boundary as a thick line, and the name of each state. How is it possible for the map to show something the satellite image cannot show, and yet the satellite image shows something a blank map could easily miss?
choices: The satellite image was taken from high altitude which allowed it to see flowing water like streams and rivers, but the altitude was too great to detect the thin line that marks a state boundary on the ground
The map shows the state boundary line because a mapmaker drew it, but the satellite image shows the stream's current shape because it is a picture of what is really there right now
The satellite can photograph only features made of solid material, so it captures streams and rivers but cannot capture abstract boundaries that exist only in law and agreement between states

The satellite image cannot show state boundaries because the boundary line is invisible on the ground itself, existing only in legal documents and on maps, whereas the stream is a physical water feature that reflects light
hints: A boundary line between two states is usually not painted on the ground, but a stream is a real physical feature.
Think about what each tool does best: one captures what is actually there at that moment, and the other can label and add lines that a person chooses to draw.

problemText: What does GPS stand for, and what is the main job of a GPS satellite?
choices: Global Position Service; satellites listen to receivers on the ground and tell them where they are
Global Positioning System; satellites send out signals that a receiver listens to in order to find a location
General Purpose Signals; satellites store maps and download them to receivers
Geo-tracking and Positioning System; satellites follow receivers and report their movement to other users
hints: Think about what a GPS satellite does — does it listen, or does it send?
The receiver is the device that does the listening. What does the satellite do?

problemText: A GPS receiver picks up a signal from a satellite directly overhead and calculates that it is 22,000 kilometers away from that satellite. Based on only this one distance, how many possible locations could the receiver be at?
choices: Exactly one location, because the receiver has calculated its distance from the satellite
Two possible locations, because circles can only cross at two points
Many possible locations forming a circle around the satellite, all at that same distance
Zero possible locations, because a receiver cannot work with just one satellite signal
hints: When you know you are a certain distance from one point in space, what shape do all those possible spots make?
Imagine drawing a circle on the ground centered at the satellite — every point on that circle is 22,000 km away from it.

problemText: A student claims that a GPS receiver needs a very strong, very clear signal from one powerful satellite to find its exact location. Is this claim correct, and why?
choices: Yes, because a strong signal gives the receiver accurate distance information from that satellite
No, because a single distance from one satellite only narrows your location to a circle, not a point, so you need distances from at least three satellites to find your exact spot
Yes, because strong signals reach further through the atmosphere than weak signals do
No, because signal strength does not add more distances to combine; the receiver still needs distances from multiple satellites
hints: What is the difference between how clear a signal is and how many satellites the receiver can pick up?
One distance — even a very accurate one — narrows your location to what shape?

problemText: A GPS receiver on a ship picks up signals from two satellites. It calculates that it is 200 km from the first satellite and 150 km from the second satellite. When the receiver draws a circle of possible spots around each satellite, the two circles cross at exactly two different points on the water. Why cannot the receiver's navigation system use this information to tell the ship captain the exact location yet?
choices: Because the receiver has not yet combined distances from enough satellites to narrow the two crossing points down to one exact spot
Because the satellites do not know where the ship is, so they cannot confirm which of the two points is the correct location on the water
Because 200 km and 150 km are not accurate enough distances to pinpoint a location on water, requiring more precise measurements from additional satellites
Because two circles cannot actually cross at exactly two points on the same plane; geometric circles can only cross at one point or not at all
hints: The lesson showed that one circle leaves many possible spots, and two circles leave two possible spots. What does it take to narrow two spots down to one?
The ship needs to add distances from at least one more satellite to eliminate one of the two crossing points.

problemText: A hiker's GPS receiver receives signals from three satellites at the same time. The receiver works out that it is 24,000 km from satellite A, 22,000 km from satellite B, and 20,000 km from satellite C. When the receiver draws all three circles and finds the one spot where all three circles meet, why does the receiver know this spot is correct?
choices: Because the three satellites sent confirmations to the receiver telling it which point to choose among all possible locations on Earth
Because the receiver tested the spot by checking that its distance to all three satellites matches the distances it calculated
Because three circles always meet at only one point, no matter what the distances are, making verification unnecessary
Because the satellites have a database of all possible locations on Earth, and they matched this one to it using triangulation mathematics
hints: How does the receiver verify that a location is correct — does it ask the satellites, or does it check something else?
Think about working backward: if the receiver measures distances from the chosen spot to all three satellites, what should those measurements show?

problemText: A navigation system receives a signal from one satellite and displays a message: "Your location is being calculated." A few seconds later, it receives a signal from a second satellite and updates the message: "Still calculating." Finally, it picks up a third satellite's signal and displays your exact location on a map. Explain why the system did not display your exact location after the second satellite's signal arrived, even though by that point it had distance information from two satellites.
choices: The second satellite's signal was weaker than the first, so the receiver could not trust the combined distances yet and had to wait for a stronger third signal to confirm
Because satellites must send their signals in a specific order, and the system was waiting for the third satellite to complete the sequence before it could work out the location

Because two distances from two satellites still narrow the location to two possible crossing points, not one exact spot; a third distance is needed to pick which of the two points is the true location
The second satellite did not know where the receiver was, so it could not narrow down the location any further than the first satellite had already done
hints: When two circles of possible spots cross each other, how many points do they share? What changes when you add a third circle?
The lesson showed that two distances alone leave two possible spots. What resolves the ambiguity?

problemText: When you are about to read a thematic map to answer a question, what should you do first before looking at any single area on the map?
choices: Look at the map's title to understand what the map is supposed to show.
Find the area that the question asks about and note its color or symbol right away.
Read every entry in the key from top to bottom so you know what each color or symbol means.
Count how many different colors or symbols appear on the map in total.
hints: The lesson emphasizes a specific routine that starts before you touch the map itself.
This first step ensures you already know the meaning of a color or symbol the moment you find it on the map.

problemText: A thematic map of the country Silverpeak shows forest coverage using three shades of green. The key states: light green means low forest coverage, medium green means medium forest coverage, and dark green means high forest coverage. On the map, Northwood is shaded dark green and Eastmoor is shaded light green. According to the key, which region has low forest coverage?
choices: Northwood, because dark green is the darkest shade on the map.
Northwood, because it appears first when you read the map from left to right.
Both regions have the same forest coverage because they are both shaded green.
Eastmoor, because the key lists light green as low forest coverage.
hints: Find the exact shade the question asks about by checking the key first.
Then match that shade to whichever region on the map is shaded that same way.

problemText: A thematic map of the country Greenmark shows each region's primary industry using symbols. The key shows: a star symbol means mining, a leaf symbol means agriculture, and a gear symbol means manufacturing. On the map, Coalton is marked with a star symbol, Plainview is marked with a leaf symbol, and Steelville is marked with a gear symbol. A student claims that Steelville must have the biggest and most important industry because the gear symbol looks the most complex. Why is this student's reasoning wrong?
choices: A symbol key shows separate categories, not a ranking, so no symbol is naturally more important than another just because it looks bigger or more complex.
The student confused visual complexity with importance, when symbol keys assign each symbol to one industry without ranking them by significance or size.
The student focused only on appearance rather than consulting the key to learn what each symbol actually represents in the legend.
The student compared symbols from different maps instead of using only the key provided for this single thematic map.
hints: Think about what a symbol key is designed to show—does it rank categories from least to most, or does it list separate, equal categories?
The size or boldness of a symbol on the map should not influence how you interpret what it means.

problemText: A thematic map of the country Waterland shows average annual rainfall using three shades of blue. The key states: light blue means low rainfall, medium blue means medium rainfall, and dark blue means high rainfall. On the map, Lakeside is shaded dark blue, Riverside is shaded medium blue, Drybrook is shaded light blue, and Marshland is shaded dark blue. How many regions have medium or high rainfall according to the key?
choices: One region (Riverside only).
Three regions (Riverside, Lakeside, and Marshland).
Two regions (Lakeside and Marshland only).
All four regions shown on the map.
hints: First, match each region's shade to the key entry that describes it.
Then count only the regions whose key entry says 'medium' or 'high'—do not count the one that says 'low'.

problemText: Two different thematic maps are displayed side by side. Map A shows temperature using three shades of red: light red means cold, medium red means warm, and dark red means hot. Map B shows ice coverage using three shades of blue: light blue means lots of ice, medium blue means some ice, and dark blue means no ice. On Map A, the Northern Zone is shaded dark red. On Map B, the Northern Zone is shaded light blue. A student asks, 'Does the dark red on Map A and the light blue on Map B mean the Northern Zone has opposite conditions?' How should you answer this question using the keys?
choices: Yes, because dark red and light blue are opposite colors on a color wheel, which always indicates opposite conditions on any map.
No, because each map uses its own separate key to define what its colors mean, so colors cannot be compared between different maps with different purposes.
Yes, because Map A's key says dark red means hot, and Map B's key says light blue means lots of ice, which are opposites.
No, because the color matching between the two maps must be the same, and you cannot check each key individually to determine meaning.
hints: Remember that each map has its own key, and you must check each key separately to find out what each color really means.
Only after you have looked up both meanings in their own keys can you decide whether the conditions are actually opposite.

problemText: A thematic map of the country Midvale shows soil type using four symbols: a plus sign means clay soil, a circle means sandy soil, a square means rocky soil, and a triangle means loamy soil. The map also displays four regions: North Field is marked with a circle, South Field is marked with a plus sign, East Field is marked with a triangle, and West Field is marked with a square. Another map of the same country shows rainfall using three shades of green: light green means low rainfall, medium green means medium rainfall, and dark green means high rainfall. According to the keys, which two regions would you predict have conditions that might both support similar kinds of plants, and why?
choices: North Field and East Field, because sandy soil and loamy soil are both found in the northern part of the country on the thematic map.
South Field and West Field, because the plus sign and square symbols appear adjacent to each other on the map's layout.
All four regions, because every region must receive identical rainfall according to how thematic maps are always structured and organized.
East Field and North Field, because East Field has loamy soil and North Field has sandy soil, and both soil types can retain some moisture.
hints: First, use the soil key to find out exactly what soil type each region has, then think about what those soil types might have in common.
The key for soil type is separate from the key for rainfall—you must use whichever key actually addresses the question being asked.

problemText: A bar graph shows the population of four towns. A longer bar on this graph represents what?
choices: A bigger area of land
A town that is farther away
A town that is older
A bigger number of people
hints: Think about what a bar graph is designed to show—the definition tells you exactly what the bar's length means.
A longer bar always stands for a bigger number in the data.

problemText: A pie chart shows how a city's 100 square kilometers of land is used for different purposes. Forests cover 35 percent of the pie chart. How many square kilometers of the city's land is covered by forests?
choices: 35 square kilometers
65 square kilometers
100 square kilometers
135 square kilometers
hints: Remember that a percent is a share of the whole. Here, the whole is 100 square kilometers.
When the whole is 100 of something, the percent number and the actual amount are the same.

problemText: A table shows rainfall amounts in three months for a city: March, 40 millimeters. April, 55 millimeters. May, 30 millimeters. How much more rainfall did April receive than May?
choices: 15 millimeters
25 millimeters
85 millimeters
95 millimeters
hints: Find the two numbers you need to compare from the table—one for April and one for May.
Subtract the smaller amount from the larger amount, and keep the unit with your answer.

problemText: A bar graph shows annual snowfall in four regions: North, 80 centimeters. South, 20 centimeters. East, 35 centimeters. West, 45 centimeters. Which two regions together received more snowfall than the other two regions combined? By how many centimeters?
choices: North and East together; 20 more centimeters
South and East together; 30 more centimeters
North and West together; 40 more centimeters
East and West together; 10 more centimeters
hints: You need to test different pairs by adding them up. Don't assume the biggest single bar is automatically part of the winning pair.
Add all four regions' totals first to check your work: the two pair totals must add up to that year total.

problemText: Two countries' pie charts show their forest coverage. Country A's pie chart shows Forests at 60 percent of A's total land area of 50 square kilometers. Country B's pie chart shows Forests at 80 percent of B's total land area of 30 square kilometers. Which country has more actual forest area in square kilometers?
choices: Country A, because 60 percent is less than 80 percent
Country B, because 80 percent is more than 60 percent
They have the same forest area because both percents are less than 100 percent
Country A, because 60 percent of 50 equals 30 square kilometers
hints: A bigger percent in one pie chart does not automatically mean a bigger amount, because the two countries' wholes may be different sizes.
Calculate the actual forest area for each country by multiplying the percent times the total land area, then compare those two amounts.

problemText: A table shows the number of endangered bird species in five regions: Region 1, 8 species. Region 2, 12 species. Region 3, 5 species. Region 4, 9 species. Region 5, 6 species. A student claims that Region 2 alone has more endangered birds than Regions 3 and 4 combined. Is the student correct? Which statement best explains why or why not?
choices: No, the student is incorrect; Regions 3 and 4 together have 14 species, which is more than Region 2's 12 species
Yes, the student is correct, because Region 2's bar would be taller than any other single bar on a bar graph
Yes, the student is correct; 12 is more than 5, so Region 2 has more species than Region 3
No, the student is incorrect; the three regions are too far apart in the table to be compared accurately
hints: A comparison question always needs two numbers read correctly and then compared. Find both numbers from the table.
Never stop at reading a single bar or region—you must add the regions you are comparing together before you can say whether the claim is true or false.
